item.title: China narrows US lead in Asia power index: report
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-23 23:09:00
China US Photo:VCG Asia Power Index 2026, released by the Australian think tank Lowy Institute, reported that the US and China are closer in power than at any time recorded. The gap in comprehensive power between the US and China — 78.9 and 73.6 respectively — continues to shrink, this year reaching its narrowest point since the inception of the Index, with the two superpowers now separated by only 5.3 points. The changing scores point to an increasingly differentiated balance of power in Asia, rather than the comprehensive dominance of either country, a Chinese observer said. While China's growing influence in several areas reflects its expanding regional engagement and capabilities, the US retains structural advantages in areas such as defence networks and future resources, underscoring that the two countries continue to hold different strengths in the region. The report said although the US and China remain the dominant countries in Asia, with just 5.3 points separating the two, the US lead over China has shrunk to its lowest level since the Asia Power Index began in 2018. It also said that China is now well ahead of the US in its diplomatic and economic relationships. The report attributed the narrowing gap "more to Washington's missteps than Beijing's advances." The US lead in military capability in Asia has been slashed due to the impact of the war on weapons stockpiles and the shift in the focus of US forces to the Middle East. Respondents to the index survey also viewed the US as increasingly distracted and disengaged from the region, the report said. The report also said that China's research and development personnel — more than triple that of the US — have driven dramatic gains across high-tech sectors. Chinese artificial intelligence (AI) models now rival their American competitors in quality, according to the report. The US' lead over China in Military Capability is at its narrowest on record. Nevertheless, Washington still retains clear advantages in defence spending, land warfare firepower, air power, and transportation capabilities, which allow it to deploy its forces and project military power across the globe. The 2026 scores highlight the distinct strengths of the two countries. China scored 98.4 in diplomatic influence and 91.8 in economic relationships, compared with 76.7 and 58 for the US. The US retained advantages in military capability, resilience, defence networks and cultural influence. The two countries were nearly level in economic capability, with the US scoring 86.7 and China 86.1, while the US held a narrower lead in future resources. "China has gained greater regional influence without seeking hegemony or deliberately pursuing an edge in major-power rivalry, reaping gains it never deliberately sought. The 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen offered a clear illustration of China's economic strength and regional engagement," an anonymous Chinese expert told the Global Times on Monday, adding that the country's growing diplomatic influence and deepening economic ties are the result of years of sustained diplomatic engagement and regional economic cooperation. China's diplomatic approach has focused on providing stable expectations and public goods through cooperation, rather than drawing ideological lines or forcing countries to choose sides, the expert said. Initiatives such as the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership and regional connectivity projects have translated diplomatic engagement into tangible economic cooperation and development opportunities. The uneven distribution of strengths also shows that regional competition has entered a more differentiated stage, rather than being a simple zero-sum contest, he said. US advantages in defence networks, military capability and cultural influence are structural assets accumulated through decades of alliance-building. Regional countries are increasingly likely to engage with major powers differently on different issues, rather than align themselves with a single camp. The narrowing gap between China and the US, alongside growing reluctance among Asia-Pacific economies to be forced to choose sides, underscores the importance of open multilateral cooperation, he said. Regional leadership is increasingly measured by the ability to safeguard free trade, provide inclusive platforms for cooperation and share development opportunities, the expert noted. India retained third place in the 2026 Asia Power Index for the third consecutive year, scoring 40.5 points, with Japan and Russia ranking fourth and fifth, respectively, Indian media platform CNBC TV18 reported. Its diplomatic influence remained its strongest measure, with a score of 70.3 points. India's economic relationships improved two places to seventh. However, its economic capability score fell 0.7 points to 26.4, despite retaining third place in that category. The expert noted that India's strategic autonomy and diversified engagement allow it to maintain flexibility in relations with major powers, while its ability to translate diplomatic influence into sustained economic growth and regional integration will be key to its future role in Asia.

item.title: GT Voice: South Korea's vehicle sector can steer clear of China deficit debate
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-23 22:37:00
An NEV manufacturing line in Southwest China's Chongqing Municipality Photo: VCG South Korea's vehicle trade deficit with China reached a record $4.231 billion in the first 10 months of this year, 4.5 times the full-year figure for 2023, according to The Chosun Daily. China's growing competitiveness in auto manufacturing is increasingly being felt in the South Korean market, but that does not mean that the two countries' economic interests are necessarily at odds. However, a more defensive view has emerged in South Korea. The Chosun Daily reported growing concerns that Chinese electric vehicles (EVs) could account for more than 50 percent of sales in South Korea next year, prompting the automotive industry to "urgently demand countermeasures." Yet there is more to this issue than competition alone. A different picture emerges from a business event in Changchun, Northeast China's Jilin Province in May. The Seoul Economic Daily reported that the Korea Trade-Investment Promotion Agency organized an export consultation as part of stepped-up efforts to help South Korean auto parts makers tap opportunities in China, where sales of eco-friendly vehicles are growing. China is an important export market for South Korean auto parts. Although China's domestic supply chain is well established, the South Korean industry sees scope to expand exports in specialized fields such as automotive electronics, software and lightweight materials. This points to another dimension of the trade that bilateral statistics rarely capture. South Korean-made components can enter China's automotive supply chains, become part of vehicles assembled by Chinese manufacturers and serve consumers in China and overseas. Some of those vehicles may even be exported back to South Korea. In trade statistics, the components are recorded as South Korean exports to China, while the finished vehicles are counted as Chinese exports to South Korea, adding to South Korea's recorded automotive trade deficit with China. Seen in this light, making the trade deficit the focus of the debate misses the point. The vehicle industries of the two neighboring countries are already intertwined through complementary strengths. As supply chains grow more complex, the distinction between trade surpluses and deficits becomes less meaningful, with companies on both sides contributing to production and benefiting from one another's markets. What South Korea's auto industry urgently needs is not a response to its trade deficit with China, let alone a demand for countermeasures. It is to strengthen its own competitiveness, move up the value chain and find new sources of growth. Put simply, the industry should be moving forward, not stopping to defend itself against China. South Korea is no newcomer to the global vehicle industry. It has established internationally recognized brands and a substantial manufacturing base. The industry put in a strong performance in October, after a period of month-to-month fluctuations. Its automobile exports rose 18.1 percent year-on-year to $6.55 billion in October, while domestic production increased 25.8 percent to 381,000 units. Vehicles are among South Korea's most important export products. The country's auto industry has long been closely connected to international markets, with overseas sales playing an important part in its development. Its next phase of growth will depend on strengthening its position in established markets while making further inroads into emerging ones. Expanding its global reach will be essential to sustaining the industry's growth. Competition between the Chinese and South Korean auto industries is real, but it is only part of the picture. There is also scope for cooperation, particularly across the parts supply chain. Such cooperation can benefit both sides, helping South Korean suppliers strengthen their competitiveness and reach customers in third-party markets. As the global auto industry moves toward electrification, the opportunities extend well beyond the two countries' bilateral trade. Emerging markets in particular offer considerable room for growth as more countries embark on the transition to electric mobility. South Korea's auto industry has little to gain from being caught up in debates over whether its trade with China is in surplus or deficit. What matters more is making better use of cooperation in regional supply chains to strengthen its own capabilities, further expand its presence in international markets and help drive the transition to electric mobility in emerging economies.

item.title: China unveils plan to boost eldercare and childcare services
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-23 22:16:00
Children play a game with childcare workers at a kindergarten in Baoying County, east China's Jiangsu Province, Nov. 10, 2026. (Xinhua/Ji Chunpeng) China's National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC), the Ministry of Civil Affairs (MCA), the National Health Commission (NHC) and the Ministry of Education jointly issued an action plan to improve services for the elderly and young children on Monday, amid efforts to respond to an aging population and alleviate the costs and pressures of raising children. The plan calls for the application of high-tech tools such as artificial intelligence (AI) and robotics to improve service quality, and supports qualified kindergartens to run nursery classes for children aged 2 to 3, as part of efforts to build both an age-friendly and birth-friendly society. The document, issued with State Council approval, follows a top-level meeting on aging-related work last week. Chinese experts said the new measures reflect fresh efforts by the Chinese government to cope with population aging, establish inclusive eldercare and childcare services, and advance exploration and practice in population governance. Tending the elderly By 2030, the layout of elderly care and childcare facilities will be more rational and better equipped, according to the plan. The integration of medical and elderly care will be further deepened, and the supply of inclusive, affordable services covering both urban and rural areas will basically take shape, as outlined in the plan. China has the world's largest elderly population. By the end of 2025, China had 323.38 million people aged 60 and above, or 23 percent of the population. The figure is projected to exceed 400 million by around 2035. "The highlight of the action plan is that it translates the broader policy goals of addressing population aging and improving childcare services into more specific and actionable measures," Yuan Xin, a professor at the Institute of Population and Development at Nankai University, told the Global Times on Monday. Specifically, the plan calls for nursing beds to account for 73 percent of all beds in elderly care institutions, and for community elderly care institutions and facilities to cover 70 percent of communities. The childcare enrollment rate for children under 3 is targeted to rise 6 percentage points from 2025 levels. The plan also prioritizes the renovation and upgrading of 2,000 outdated public elderly care institutions to improve professional care capacity and safety management. The targets of 73 percent nursing beds and 70 percent community coverage signal a shift toward more specialized and community-based services, Yuan said. Many older people prefer to remain at home and in familiar communities, making accessible community support particularly important. The focus should be on providing professional medical and nursing care for older people with disabilities, while helping healthier seniors maintain independent lives for as long as possible, the expert added. The plan encourages elderly care and childcare institutions to adopt smart management platforms, intelligent fire safety and security systems, and equips elderly care facilities with smart health monitoring devices and assistive tools. It also promotes AI agents, service robots, smart wearables and exoskeletons in elderly care scenarios, and supports setting up experience zones in care institutions and communities. The plan is part of a series of government directives rolled out in recent years as China experiences a rapidly aging population. Further efforts were urged to implement the national strategy of actively addressing population aging and to ensure happier and more fulfilling lives for elderly people at a recent instruction on work related to aging, Xinhua reported. The meeting called for coordinating efforts among the government, market, society and families, and further strengthening social security, elderly care services, health services and social participation for older people, while stressing the need to boost the silver economy and build an age-friendly society. Improving childcare Some of the outlined measures, such as encouraging qualified kindergartens to offer nursery classes for children aged 2, became trending topics on Chinese social media on Monday. "This policy is really practical for dual-income families like us. I had my baby in February 2026. In some places, new mothers can apply for extended leave until the baby turns one with their employer's approval, but maternity benefits in Beijing end much earlier. If kindergartens can offer childcare for two-year-olds, such support will be extended, filling the gap between the end of leave and the child turning three. I hope suitable spots become available nearby soon," a Beijing-based white-collar worker surnamed Huo told the Global Times on Monday. According to the plan, the country supports qualified kindergartens in renovating and expanding facilities to offer nursery classes for children aged 2 to 3, addressing public concerns over parenting difficulties. Childcare facilities will be properly distributed to build a "15-minute childcare service circle." Challenges remain, however. Expanding nursery classes to 2-year-olds requires retraining kindergarten teachers who are unaccustomed to toddler care, while reaching 70 percent community elderly care coverage hinges on sustained funding at the county level - a hurdle for less prosperous regions, analysts said. The latest directives reflect a growing recognition that improving childcare accessibility is essential to easing the burden on young families and supporting their willingness to have children, Yuan said. "While population aging is an irreversible demographic trend, fertility remains a key factor shaping China's future population structure." The country's natural population growth rate stood at minus 2.41 per thousand in 2025, with 11.31 million deaths. China's total population reached 1.40489 billion at the end of 2025, down 3.39 million from a year earlier, data with the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) showed. The average size of Chinese households also fell to 2.52 people per household in 2025, 0.58 fewer than a decade ago. Top-down push The plan announced on Monday is consistent with the central government's directives to develop the silver economy and bolster consumption of elderly care services. China faces three major trends: an aging population, rising incomes and downward pressure on economic growth. Elderly care and childcare, as components of the broader health industry, offer new growth opportunities, Cao Heping, a professor at Peking University, told the Global Times on Monday. Policies addressing aging foster the health industry's development, meeting demand for healthcare, rehabilitation and elderly care while creating new sources of economic growth and employment, he noted. With a rapidly aging population, the traditional family-based elderly care system is facing challenges. As a socialist country, tending to senior citizens is a key government task, and timely policy rollout plays a crucial role in guiding social resources, Bian Yongzu, a senior researcher at the China Institutes of Contemporary International Relations, told the Global Times on Monday. Bian noted that with the ascent of China's AI technology and robotics industry, industry insiders generally agree that robots will soon handle most daily tasks needed by the elderly. "AI allows people to communicate smoothly with robots without needing PC or internet skills," Bian said. With policy support and economies of scale, the costs of AI-powered elderly care robots will fall to levels most Chinese households can afford in the not-too-distant future. Companion robots, exoskeletons, fall detection systems and smart wearables can help older people overcome mobility and safety challenges, Yuan said, predicting that intelligent devices will become common in home-based, community and institutional elderly care over the next five to 10 years. According to a blue paper on China's silver economy, China's silver economy is currently valued at 7 trillion yuan, with tourism as a key growth area, and the sector is projected to reach 30 trillion yuan by 2035.

item.title: Chinese PLA steps up joint training among Navy, Air Force and Rocket Force to strengthen integrated operational capabilities
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-23 20:38:00
PLA Navy guided-missile destroyer Zibo sails on the sea. Photo: 81.cn The Chinese People's Liberation Army (PLA) is stepping up efforts to promote joint training among its military services, with a PLA Navy destroyer flotilla opening up its maritime training resources to Air Force and Rocket Force units, according to a report from the PLA Daily. Such efforts are seen as an important step toward building a world-class military by strengthening the PLA's joint operational capabilities and improving coordination among its services, experts noted. During a recent maritime exercise aboard the PLA Navy guided-missile destroyer Zibo , naval personnel identified gaps in their ability to detect very-low-altitude targets under certain sea conditions and electronic jamming scenarios. Air Force officer Wei Yufeng, drawing on his perspective as an aerial attacker, offered suggestions for improving the formation's air defense positioning and the timing of fire coordination, according to the PLA Daily report. Wei also served as a cross-service staff officer during the exercise, helping the ship's crew assess the air situation. His participation brought an Air Force perspective into the Navy's training and reviews, allowing naval personnel to examine their air-defense arrangements from the perspective of an aerial attacker. The waters were once used primarily by the Navy, but under an initiative to open up training to other services, Air Force aircraft and Rocket Force units have increasingly joined exercises in the area. Maritime training grounds are no longer used exclusively by the Navy but have become a shared venue where personnel from different services can train together, improve coordination and test their capabilities. The exercise gave personnel from the two services a better understanding of each other's capabilities and operational requirements. Previous joint exercises had exposed gaps in coordination, including difficulties in aligning air strikes with naval air-defense operations and directing timely strikes against maneuvering maritime targets, according to the report. To address these gaps, the task force has incorporated its annual training plan into a broader joint training program, reporting available maritime training areas and time slots, electromagnetic environments, simulated opposing forces and support resources to higher-level authorities for allocation. Other services can submit specific training requests, which a dedicated team then coordinates and integrates into joint exercises. Regular joint training has helped personnel better understand operational capabilities, an officer with a PLA Navy unit affiliated with the Eastern Theater Command told the PLA Daily. Air Force officers have learned about the detection limits of naval radar, while naval commanders have gained a better understanding of air-strike tactics and vulnerabilities, the officer said. The key to improving joint operations lies not only in upgrading equipment, but also in breaking down barriers over the use of training resources and making them serve broader operational needs, the officer said. "Modern warfare can break out at any time and in any place, including across different maritime areas. While the PLA previously needed a longer period to prepare for operations, that preparation time has now been significantly shortened. This reflects the continuous improvement and upgrading of its information systems and command structures," Song Zhongping, a military affairs expert, told the Global Times. According to Song, joint operations involving the Navy, Air Force and Rocket Force are particularly important because modern warfare cannot be fought by a single service acting alone. It requires different services to work together through integrated command and data-link systems. "There is still work to be done to further improve and upgrade these systems, ensuring that different services can operate on a unified data network and be brought together when needed to conduct joint operations across different domains, at any time and in any location. This is where the practical value of joint operations lies," noted Song. The initiative builds on a longer-term effort to integrate the PLA's forces and improve their ability to operate together. The effort is part of the PLA's broader push to strengthen joint operations. China's 2015 white paper on military strategy called for gradually establishing an integrated joint operational system, bringing different operational forces, units and elements together through information systems. The country has formulated a three-step development strategy for modernizing national defense and the armed forces, with the aim of achieving the centenary objectives of the PLA by 2027, basically realizing the modernization of national defense and the armed forces by 2035, and fully building the armed forces into world-class forces by the mid-21st century, according to the white paper. According to Song, the PLA has continued to make progress in strengthening its information capabilities and improving coordination among its military services. It is also making greater use of information and intelligent technologies to enhance its operational capabilities. "Further efforts are needed to deepen the integration of different services and build a more unified and efficient joint operational system," he said.

item.title: When Japan needs a magnifying glass to find itself in a White House video
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-23 20:32:00
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi leaves the stage after leaders pose for a group photo during the APEC meeting in Shenzhen, China, on 19 November, 2026. Photo: VCG How does a country celebrate its diplomatic achievements? Japan recently offered a rather unusual answer. The country's Cabinet Secretary for Public Affairs recently posted a White House press conference video, zeroed in on the 13:58 mark, and triumphantly noted that Japan got a mention, and was called a "friend." Apparently, Tokyo was worried the rest of the world might miss the big news that the US still remembers Japan. While other countries are busy securing major agreements, breakthroughs on regional issues, or tangible benefits for their people from multilateral diplomacy, Japan seems increasingly eager to prove just one thing: that Washington still considers Tokyo a friend. This kind of diplomatic messaging is hard not to see as black humor. This "13:58 diplomacy" is less a triumph than a symptom of the deepening anxiety inside the Sanae Takaichi administration. People often talk most about what they feel they lack. A look at Takaichi's performance at the recent APEC meeting makes the awkwardness plain to see. A widely circulated video shows Takaichi hurrying over to US President Donald Trump after the group photo of APEC leaders, then giving him a pat on the back. Trump barely glanced at her before turning away and walking off. Some Japanese viewers said on social media that they felt embarrassed. Others also expressed disappointment with Takaichi's facial expressions and body language during the meetings, including grimacing and sticking out her tongue. They questioned whether such behavior was appropriate for a national leader on the diplomatic stage. Others pointed out that while leaders gathered in small groups to talk, Takaichi appeared to be sitting alone, missing opportunities to exchange views and build relationships on the sidelines of the gatherings. Against this backdrop, the Cabinet Secretary for Public Affairs' tweet looks more like an attempt to reassure the domestic audience. Even before the Shenzhen APEC meeting, the Japanese side had shown obvious sensitivity about how Takaichi might be treated during her visit to China, repeatedly fretting about the possibility of a cold reception, differential treatment, and reading supposed diplomatic signals into every minor detail. In the end, she received a red-carpet welcome, a guard of honor, along with the usual diplomatic courtesies. As host, China provided arrangements fully in line with international practice. Yet what ultimately determines a country's international standing is not how long a red carpet others roll out for you, but how much real weight you yourself carry. Unfortunately, Japan hasn't figured that out yet. Most countries in the Asia-Pacific want to focus on economic development and regional cooperation. Japan, by contrast, keeps framing regional issues in military terms. While others look for opportunities to cooperate, some Japanese politicians remain busy stoking strategic confrontation. As countries across the region pursue peace, development and shared interests, Japanese policy is moving further toward re-militarization. Tokyo seems to want to earn the trust of its regional neighbors, yet keeps eroding that trust. It positions itself as a key supporter and defender of a free and open international order grounded in the rule of law, yet pushes the region toward confrontation. This strategic contradiction is a major reason why Japan's diplomatic room for maneuver is narrowing. The real question for Japan is not whether the US president mentioned it at a press conference, but why it is so desperate for Washington's approval while failing so badly to win the trust of its own neighbors through clear-eyed policy. Unfortunately, Tokyo has become so desperate for attention that it now fixates on the smallest details - even the exact second Japan is mentioned in a White House video. The more it obsesses over such trivialities, the more it reveals how little it has to show for itself. Thirteen minutes and fifty-eight seconds is short - short enough for the White House to give Japan just one brief mention. Yet it is also long - long enough for the outside world to see the growing gap between Japan's diplomatic ambitions and its actual standing on the global stage. Politicians can build strong images at home through carefully crafted messaging, but on the international stage, what matters to others is their actual weight, policy credibility, and value as a partner. Real diplomatic weight doesn't need others to mention you just to feel relevant. It makes others take your positions, interests, and choices seriously. That's true dignity - not replaying a White House video, checking once again: America, do you still remember me?

item.title: China's flu activity reaches moderate level, with three strains circulating simultaneously: reports
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-23 13:30:00
Photo: Screenshot from CCTV News China's latest influenza surveillance data indicate that flu activity nationwide has reached a moderate level, with three strains circulating at the same time this season, according to media reports. Medical experts said that the flu vaccine offers protection against all three strains, underscoring the importance of boosting vaccination rates and raising public awareness of the vaccine. Northern China has seen a sharp rise in flu positivity rates, while southern regions remain at fluctuating levels of activity, with clustered outbreaks increasing from the previous period, according to data released by the Chinese Center for Disease Control and Prevention, CCTV News reported. A notable feature of this year's flu season is the simultaneous circulation of three influenza strains - A(H1N1), A(H3N2) and B(Victoria) - with their respective proportions continuing to shift, the report said. In October, A(H3N2) was overwhelmingly dominant. By November, however, the proportion of A(H1N1) had risen steadily, making it the predominant strain, while A(H3N2) had fallen to below 20 percent. B(Victoria), meanwhile, has maintained a relatively stable share and continued to circulate. The coexistence of multiple influenza strains and the rapid shift in the predominant strain are the most notable features of this year's flu season, posing new challenges for prevention, CCTV said. The risk of being infected by different flu strains in succession has increased, as cross-protection among influenza strains is relatively weak, said Li Tongzeng, a chief physician with the respiratory and infectious diseases department at Beijing You'an Hospital. "For example, contracting influenza A does not rule out a subsequent influenza B infection, while infection with A(H3N2) offers limited protection against A(H1N1), leaving people susceptible to reinfection with a different strain," he added, according to the CCTV report. Li recommended vaccination, noting that the trivalent influenza vaccine offers protection against all three circulating viruses. For the general public, there is little need to focus too much on whether an infection is influenza A or B, as their clinical symptoms are similar, including fever, headache, sore throat, cough, muscle aches and pronounced fatigue, the expert noted. Influenza A and B viruses circulate every year, and existing flu vaccines provide protection against both, President of Shenzhen Third People's Hospital Lu Hongzhou told the Global Times on Monday. The priority in China, therefore, is to increase annual influenza vaccination rates and strengthen public awareness through science-based public health education. Also, existing antiviral medications are effective against both influenza A and B. The key is to obtain an early diagnosis, confirm whether the infection is influenza, and begin treatment promptly, Lu added.

item.title: HKSAR Election Committee polls highlight strengths of new electoral system, high-quality democracy: central authorities
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-23 12:06:00
The 2026 Election Committee Subsector Ordinary Elections of Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (HKSAR) was successfully held on November 22, 2026. Photo: Screenshot from news.gov.hk The 2026 Election Committee Subsector Ordinary Elections in the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (HKSAR) were successfully held on Sunday, recording a 98.79 percent turnout, with 5,640 people voting. The election fully upheld the principle of "patriots administering Hong Kong" and highlighted the strengths of the city's new electoral system, marking another important step in advancing democracy with Hong Kong characteristics, a spokesperson for the Liaison Office of Central Government in the HKSAR said on Monday. The HKSAR Chief Executive John Lee on Sunday congratulated those elected, describing the poll as an example of healthy competition among patriots. He urged the new members to contribute to the long-term success of the "One Country, Two Systems" principle. Liang Haiming, chairman of the China Silk Road iValley Research Institute and dean of the Belt and Road Research Institute at Hainan University, told the Global Times on Monday that the new electoral system has three key strengths: establishing a common political foundation under the principle of "patriots administering Hong Kong" while safeguarding constitutional order; promoting balanced participation by accommodating the interests of different sectors; and enhancing political effectiveness by encouraging candidates to compete on the basis of their policy platforms, capabilities and performance. According to Liang, the key to developing democracy with Hong Kong characteristics lies in upholding "One Country, Two Systems," taking local circumstances into account, and improving governance effectiveness. The new electoral system aims to ensure the selection of capable leaders, address public concerns and translate institutional strengths into tangible improvements in people's livelihoods and social stability. The spokesperson of the liaison office said the elections were held at a significant time as HKSAR entered a new stage in implementing "One Country, Two Systems," rolled out its first five-year plan and prepared to mark the 30th anniversary of its return to China. The new members, whose term largely coincides with the five-year plan's implementation period, are expected to help the HKSAR government turn its development vision into reality, amid strong public attention and expectations. According to Liang, the new members can help provide policy continuity and align national development priorities with Hong Kong's strengths in finance, innovation and technology, and shipping, while addressing local needs in housing, employment and elderly care. The elections demonstrated the strengths of Hong Kong's new electoral system, including broad representation, political inclusiveness, balanced participation and fair competition. A total of 31 subsectors saw more candidates than available seats, with some recording contests of 25 candidates for 15 seats and 23 for 15, according to the spokesperson. According to the spokesperson, the diverse backgrounds of the candidates, ranging from young professionals and academics to Olympic medalists, musicians with disabilities and foreign bank executives, demonstrated balanced participation and merit-based selection. Li Xiaobing, a Hong Kong, Macao and Taiwan affairs expert from Nankai University, said the figures demonstrate broader and more extensive democratic participation, with more people willing to engage in the electoral process. The members drawn from Hong Kong's political, cultural, business and professional sectors represent key forces in the city's development. As a foundational institution in association with the chief executive election and the Legislative Council's nomination and election processes, the committee's active participation reflects confidence in Hong Kong's political future and development, Li told the Global Times on Monday.

item.title: Type 075, Type 055 and Type 054A warships to open to public at 16th Airshow China: PLA Navy
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-23 11:20:00
Up: The Chinese People's Liberation Army Navy's Type 075 amphibious assault ship Hubei Photo: PLA Southern Theater Command Down left: A Type 054A frigate Down right: A Type 055 destroyer Photos: VCG The PLA Navy on Monday released its lineup for the 16th China International Aviation and Aerospace Exhibition (Airshow China 2026), which includes the Type 075 amphibious assault ship, the Type 055 large destroyer and the Type 054A frigate. Experts on military affairs told the Global Times that the star-studded display features three major highlights: the "five carrier-related assets," nearly 10 types of new main combat equipment, and a combined display of surface vessels, carrier-based jets and marine forces, showcasing the navy's systemic combat prowess. Under a coordinated arrangement, the PLA Navy will showcase a mix of actual hardware and scale models in four categories: indoor exhibitions, outdoor static displays, flight demonstrations and vessel open-house visits. The exhibits will include main combat warships, carrier-based fighter jets, carrier-borne helicopters, anti-submarine patrol aircraft, shipborne weapon systems and armored equipment, according to the PLA Navy. New-generation main combat vessels, including the Type 075 amphibious assault ship, the Type 055 guided-missile destroyer and the Type 054A guided-missile frigate, will be open to the public at Gaolan Port. The outdoor static display area will also feature new aircraft such as the J-15T carrier-based fighter, the Z-20F carrier-borne anti-submarine helicopter, the Y-9 anti-submarine patrol aircraft and the WZ-2 unmanned helicopter. For the flight demonstrations, the PLA Navy will deploy the J-35 carrier-based stealth fighter jet, the J-15T carrier-based heavy fighter, the KJ-600 early warning aircraft, and the JL-15 trainer aircraft, as well as the Z-20J and Z-8C helicopters. They will perform formation flypasts, low-level passes and airfield raid drills, offering a multi-dimensional showcase of the PLA Navy's maritime and aerial combat system. Thirty years have passed since the China Airshow was first held in Zhuhai in 1996. The PLA Navy brought physical equipment to the 15th Airshow for the first time in 2024. This year's edition marks the launch of a new offshore exhibition zone at Gaolan Port, where a large formation of active-duty naval vessels is set to be on display, according to experts. "For the first time, this Airshow opens the offshore exhibition area at Gaolan Port, where the PLA Navy's main combat ships will make their debut at the Zhuhai Airshow. Its greatest significance lies in breaking the previous limitation of the Airshow, which largely focused on aerial hardware, enabling the simultaneous display of naval, land, air and space equipment," Zhang Junshe, a military affairs expert told the Global Times on Monday. Previous editions of the Airshow focused primarily on aerial assets. The newly added naval vessel segment fills a critical gap in the maritime dimension, delivering a more comprehensive exhibition framework. Visitors can get up close to active-duty warships and book tours on board, offering a more immersive, firsthand viewing experience than past displays, which were limited to scale models, said Zhang. "The concentrated participation of naval equipment further broadens the international profile of Airshow China in Zhuhai and elevates its global standing. It also fully demonstrates China's robust capacity to host a large-scale defense expo covering land, sea, air and space domains," the expert said. All three surface combatants at the Gaolan Port maritime exhibition zone - the Type 075 amphibious assault ship, the Type 055 large destroyer and the Type 054A frigate - are making their debut at Airshow China. Among the aerial contingent, the J-35, KJ-600, Z-20F, Y-9 anti-submarine patrol aircraft, JL-15 and WZ-2 unmanned helicopter are also participating in the expo for the first time. Compared to the PLA Navy's debut at Airshow China in 2024, the navy is fielding three types of main combat warships and nearly 10 types of aircraft this year, forming an exceptionally strong lineup, Zhang said. Zhang outlined three standout highlights of the naval display. Topping the list is the first-ever public tour of the Type 055 10,000-ton-class destroyer. As China's first domestically built destroyer of this displacement class, the vessel is known as the "sword-bearing guard" for carrier strike groups. It incorporates breakthroughs in overall design and information integration. As a landmark platform symbolizing China's transition from offshore defense to far-sea operations, it stands among the world's most capable surface combatants. The second highlight is the complete lineup of the "five carrier-related assets" on show in Zhuhai. The suite includes the J-35 stealth carrier-based fighter, catapult-launched J-15T multirole carrier fighter, KJ-600 carrier-borne early warning aircraft, J-15DT carrier-based electronic warfare jet and Z-20F carrier anti-submarine helicopter. Third, unmanned systems headlined by the WZ-2 unmanned helicopter are appearing alongside unmanned surface vessels and other unmanned hardware. Taken together, these three highlights offer a comprehensive picture of the PLA Navy's evolving capabilities in far-sea defense, system-of-systems warfare and intelligent unmanned operations. The guided-missile destroyer Dalian (Hull 105) attached to the PLA Southern Theater Command sails during a far-sea joint training drill in early April, 2023. Photo: eng.chinamil.com.cn "The J-35, KJ-600 and Z-20F are all making their debut at Airshow China. Among them, the Z-20F carrier-based anti-submarine helicopter is appearing at an airshow for the first time and is being unveiled to the public for the very first time. This marks the public debut of all five domestically developed carrier-related assets," said Zhang, adding that the completion of this carrier-based aviation system will further strengthen the overall combat capabilities of China's carrier strike groups. According to official information, compared with previous airshow, the PLA Navy is placing greater emphasis on combat-oriented training this time. All exhibited items are active-duty main combat assets that regularly operate in the open ocean, carrying out combat readiness training, exercises and maritime rights protection missions. These are not static exhibits but warfighting hardware operating across the blue waters, vividly demonstrating the PLA Navy's operational readiness. The exhibition also highlights new-quality capabilities and emerging domains. It showcases a suite of next-generation platforms that have just entered service, received design certification or attained initial operational capability. The concentrated display of active-duty main warships offers a direct glimpse of the navy's robust open-ocean combat strength, testifying to the accelerated transformation of the navy amid the drive to strengthen the military in the new era. Systemic integration is another key focus. For the first time, the complete "vessel platform plus carrier-based aviation" system is presented together. Multiple newly upgraded and newly developed carrier-based fighters, early warning aircraft and helicopters make their collective debut. Displayed alongside major destroyers and frigates, amphibious warfare assets and coastal-sea defense systems, they illustrate the full maritime-air combat architecture of a carrier strike group. Greater prominence is also given to unmanned and intelligent systems. Unmanned aerial vehicles, unmanned underwater vehicles and other unmanned platforms and scale models will be on display, reflecting the PLA Navy's cutting-edge research into unmanned and intelligent warfare and pointing to emerging modes of future maritime combat.

item.title: As Chinese universities use AI detectors to screen theses, questions arise over accuracy
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-23 09:55:00
Students communicate at the Wangjiang Campus of Sichuan University in Chengdu, southwest China's Sichuan Province, Sept. 29, 2026. (Xinhua/Wang Xi) After five rounds of revisions, one student still had a thesis flagged as 30 percent AI-generated by an artificial intelligence (AI) detector. Such results have become a source of anxiety for many graduating students in China. As AI detection tools become more widely used in thesis reviews, some universities have made the "AI rate" a formal requirement alongside conventional plagiarism checks. A paper that passes the plagiarism check can still be barred from thesis defense if its AI rate exceeds the permitted threshold. But the reliability of this technology is increasingly in question. Some detection platforms have flagged passages from classic Chinese literary works, including Zhu Ziqing's "Moonlight over the Lotus Pond" and writings by Lu Xun, as more than 80 percent AI-generated. These cases highlight a problem facing universities as they try to regulate generative AI: a single percentage says little about how much intellectual work a student has actually done. Four scholars in the fields of law, communication and education, speaking to Xinhua, said the AI rate should not serve as a decisive standard. WHY DETECTORS ARE INCONSISTENT Commercial AI detectors use AI to identify AI-generated writing, said Zhang Linghan, head of the institute of AI law at China University of Political Science and Law. They analyze statistical features such as perplexity and burstiness, assuming that machine-generated prose is unusually fluent and standardized while human writing varies in rhythm. Given the probabilistic method, no tool is fully accurate, she said, and a percentage alone "cannot serve as reliable evidence of academic misconduct." Wang Feng, dean of the School of Communication at East China Normal University, said AI detection differs fundamentally from plagiarism screening. Plagiarism checks compare papers against existing texts and identify sources of overlap. AI detectors, by contrast, rely on algorithmic rules rather than traceable source texts. Results can vary across platforms using different data and algorithms, and can even differ when the same paper is submitted to the same platform at different times, he said. Classic works can be flagged because the stylistic conventions detectors treat as markers of AI writing largely derive from classic literature, Wang added. Xiong Bingqi, head of the 21st Century Education Research Institute in Shenzhen, south China, noted that plagiarism checks, introduced in China more than 20 years ago, had never resolved questions of originality: students could evade them by rewording or rearranging borrowed text. AI detectors, he said, similarly cannot determine whether a paper is original or innovative. WHERE THE LINE IS The limits of detection matter because students may use AI to search academic literature, polish language, draft an outline or generate an entire paper -- activities with very different academic implications that current detection tools cannot distinguish. Zhang said the key question is whether the student's own contribution remains "substantive and dominant." Using AI for literature searches, language polishing or formatting generally should not be treated as misconduct and may need no or only brief disclosure, she said. AI-generated outlines are also generally acceptable, provided students check them for factual errors. But if AI contributes to a paper's core ideas or directly generates text used in its main body, such use must be disclosed, she said. Students are seen at a library inside the Shipai campus of Jinan University in Guangzhou, south China's Guangdong Province, Nov. 11, 2026. (Xinhua/Deng Hua) Wang, whose university was among the first in China to issue guidelines on students' use of AI, said East China Normal University initially set a 20-percent limit on directly generated content. The limit applied only to text used without subsequent changes, while text students revised and adapted to their research should not count as directly generated. He also cautioned against judging papers based on their so-called AI feel: scientific writing is often formulaic, and academic value should rest on originality, not prose style. Chu Zhaohui, a research fellow at the China National Academy of Educational Sciences, stressed that AI cannot replace original research based on real circumstances, experiments and data. He cited two instances in which AI had fabricated material: a sentence generated by AI and circulated online under his name, and a student assignment citing a nonexistent article attributed to him, complete with a title, journal name and page numbers. Despite these limitations, many Chinese universities have adopted percentage limits on the "AI rate" because they are relatively easy to administer and can serve as a deterrent, Zhang said. But she warned that the thresholds lack strong scientific support, risk penalizing legitimate AI use and have fueled a gray market in services promising to lower AI-detection scores. Rigid scoring rules can also push students into meaningless rewriting just to lower their AI scores, Zhang said. A better approach, she argued, would allow AI use with transparent disclosure, strengthen process-based evaluation and adviser oversight, and gradually reduce reliance on a single quantitative measure. WHAT A THESIS SHOULD MEASURE The debate over AI detection ultimately raises a more fundamental question: what should a university thesis demonstrate? For Chu, the central issue is not AI but evaluation itself. A good paper should address questions others have not explored or offer insights that advance existing understanding, he said. Theses built on repetition, piles of references or superficial formalities had little value even before AI, and the technology has only made their weaknesses more apparent. Universities, he said, should give greater weight to process-based evaluation while also assessing the final work for its research substance and by the standards of the academic community. Zhang called for combining institutional rules with human judgment. Universities should assess students throughout the research process, from topic selection and research proposals to fieldwork, writing and the final defense, she said. Substantive judgments about a paper's originality, rigor and research value should be left to advisers and peer experts, with an appeals process for disputed decisions. Xiong said closer supervision could also reduce reliance on detection tools. Advisers who follow students from topic selection through research and writing can identify many problems before a thesis is completed. Wang emphasized the role of teachers in making this shift work. Rather than simply barring students from using AI, universities should invest more in improving teachers' AI literacy and exploring how the technology can be integrated into teaching and research. Teachers, he said, should help students explore appropriate uses of AI, guide them in its application and provide academic oversight. The four scholars' views converge on one conclusion: academic integrity cannot be reduced to a numerical score. A thesis should be judged not by whether a student stays below an AI rate threshold, but by whether the student can pose meaningful questions, investigate them via genuine research and arrive at independent conclusions.

item.title: The world is talking about Shenzhen – what are they talking about?: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-22 21:52:00
APEC China 2026. Illustration: Liu Rui/GT Viewed from the world's perspective, Western developed countries are not only observing where China is headed but also reflecting on what they may have missed. Developing nations are examining what kinds of urban lifestyles and industrial development can become a reality, and whether the path to industrialization must necessarily follow the old path of "polluting first, then cleaning up." Shenzhen is not the sole answer to the future, yet it proves there is more than one path forward. Over the past week, Shenzhen has undoubtedly stood at the center of the world's spotlight. In media reports from around the globe - ranging from its densely packed skyscrapers to self-driving taxis on the streets - Shenzhen has been portrayed as a "futuristic city." Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney praised Shenzhen, saying, "The future is designed here, tested here and built here." US President Donald Trump noted that Shenzhen is "clean" and "immaculate," adding that, in contrast, the development and governance of some US cities are "embarrassing." Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori stated that "there is no doubt that we can learn from Shenzhen" in its approach to smart and digital urban governance. On overseas social media platforms, "Shenzhen" continues to dominate the feed. One netizen wrote, "This might be the most futuristic city I've ever visited in my life," while another added, "I wish my country could have a Shenzhen too." Why has a once remote fishing village attracted so much attention? When the world talks about Shenzhen, what exactly are they talking about? Perhaps the answer lies in one word: future. Seen from within China, Shenzhen embodies the concrete form of Chinese modernization, offering a vivid interpretation of the idea that "the next 'China' is still China." When the Special Economic Zone was established in 1980, Shenzhen's population was less than 30,000. Now, it has developed into a modern international metropolis and "super hub" with a population of over 18 million. Today, people here see self-driving cars cruising the streets, drone deliveries becoming part of daily life, robots operating in factories and shopping malls, and companies like Huawei, BYD, DJI, and Tencent making their mark on the global market. Behind these achievements lie China's sustained investment and stable planning - rooted in its own development and oriented toward the future - and, ultimately, a people-centered approach to development. Viewed from the world's perspective, Western developed countries are not only observing where China is headed but also reflecting on what they may have missed. A key reason why Trump's assessment of Shenzhen's roads and urban environment sparked debate in US public opinion is that it touched on the long-standing challenges of urban governance facing American society. Road maintenance, public transportation, and environmental sanitation - these seemingly ordinary public services are, in fact, persistent challenges that many countries struggle to address. Developing nations, meanwhile, are examining what kinds of urban lifestyles and industrial development can become a reality, and whether the path to industrialization must necessarily follow the old path of "polluting first, then cleaning up." Whether developed or developing, countries are beginning to consider whether they should pursue this kind of future. Shenzhen is not the sole answer to the future, yet it proves that there is more than one path forward. Different countries have different historical traditions, cultural practices, resource endowments, and social systems; there can be no single "standard answer" for urban modernization. Nor is Shenzhen's path a template that can be simply replicated. Its significance lies in demonstrating that openness can spur innovation, industry can foster technology, technology can improve lives, and global cooperation can expand the scope for development. Chilean President Jose Antonio Kast remarked, "Shenzhen's transformation reminds us that progress is not a miracle but a resolution." Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, drawing on his experiences from visits in 1998 and 2026, remarked that if someone were to place photographs from then and now side by side, it was almost impossible to believe they were of the same place. This demonstrates that the future can be continuously shaped through reform, opening-up, and relentless exploration. What the world needs is not a replica of Shenzhen, but more cities like Shenzhen that can shape their own futures. Today, Shenzhen has evolved from a place where the Chinese people learned about the world through the "window of the world" to a place where the world observes China and envisions the future. In just over 40 years, Shenzhen has traversed a journey that took some major international metropolises abroad more than a century to complete, proving that modernization does not follow a single predetermined path. A late-developing economy can fully forge its own path - one that balances efficiency with people's livelihoods, and vitality with order. This demonstrates that the "future" is not merely a fixed blueprint. Every country and every civilization can draw upon its own historical traditions, social structures, and resource endowments to find a "future blueprint" that suits it best. British urban planning scholar Peter Hall once wrote Cities of Tomorrow, which traces urban planning practices from the late 19th century to the late 20th century - a work in which London, New York, Paris, and Chicago frequently feature. Today, one "city of tomorrow" after another is emerging across China. We welcome more countries, enterprises, research institutions, and innovators to come to Shenzhen. Rather than merely viewing a single "pre-existing model," we can strive to build more models and explore abundant future forms of AI, green development, urban governance, public services, and industrial cooperation. Shenzhen's story is far from finished, and the exploration of Chinese modernization is still underway. The invitation Shenzhen extends to the world is this: China is willing to showcase its own future, and welcomes the world to bring its own dreams here to jointly create even more bright futures.
